title: Amplitude
subtitle: Play the song by moving between its parts

body: Amplitude is Harmonix's PlayStation 2 rhythm game, first released in North America on 25 March 2003. A beat-blaster ship travels along lanes representing different instruments, and the player strikes note patterns in time with the music. Completing one part allows attention to move elsewhere in the arrangement. The activity turns a recording into several related tasks, each asking for the same sense of timing in a different pattern. As the sequel to FreQuency, it develops Harmonix's early idea of making the listener responsible for how a song comes together.

Accurate sequences raise the score and build a multiplier, rewarding sustained control rather than a single difficult input. Missed notes drain energy and can end the song before it finishes. Moving between the six musical tracks adds another decision to the immediate rhythm: the player must choose where to act while keeping time with the part already in front of them. A song becomes more familiar through repeated attempts, as its instrumental layers turn into recognisable shapes and the next transition can be anticipated rather than merely reacted to.

Amplitude broadened FreQuency's electronic emphasis with more pop and rock material, giving the same underlying play a wider range of musical textures. Greg LoPiccolo directed the project for Harmonix, before the studio's later success with Guitar Hero and Rock Band. Its critical reception helped establish the team as a specialist in music games. Harmonix returned to the name with a crowdfunded reboot released in 2016. The original shows an earlier route into that field, using an ordinary controller to let the player move through the separate layers of a finished recording.
